title: Streamlit Reference
text:
Launch from the project root
uv sync
uv run streamlit run app.py
Leave the terminal open. Ctrl+C stops the server. Streamlit scripts run through the terminal, rather than as ordinary notebook cells.

title: Streamlit Reference
text:
Display information
import streamlit as st

st.title("Conference Message Explorer")
st.header("Explore the sample")
st.subheader("Read a message")
st.write("Text, numbers, or other objects")
st.markdown("**Important context**")
st.caption("52 selected kickers, not the complete archive")
st.metric("Talks displayed", 16)
st.dataframe(df, hide_index=True)
print(...) writes to the server’s terminal or logs. st.write(...) displays in the browser. Use explicit Streamlit display calls while learning.

title: Streamlit Reference
text:
Inputs return Python values
year = st.selectbox("Year", [2020, 2023, 2025])
years = st.multiselect("Years", [2020, 2023, 2025], default=[2025])
earliest = st.select_slider("Earliest year", [2020, 2023, 2025])
n = st.slider("Number to show", min_value=1, max_value=10, value=5)
text = st.text_input("Words in the title")
show_table = st.checkbox("Show supporting records", value=True)

shown = df.loc[df["year"].isin(years)]
if show_table:
    st.dataframe(shown)
In the basic execution model, committing a widget change reruns the script from top to bottom. A text input normally commits when the reader presses Enter or leaves the field. Plotly hover and zoom remain browser interactions unless the app explicitly connects supported events to Python.

title: Streamlit Reference
text:
Charts
st.bar_chart(shown.groupby("year").size().rename("Talks"))

import plotly.express as px
fig = px.scatter(shown, x="PHATE1", y="PHATE2",
                 color="role_group", hover_name="title")
st.plotly_chart(fig, width="stretch")

# For a Matplotlib or Seaborn figure:
st.pyplot(fig_matplotlib)
Plotly builds the interactive figure. Streamlit connects it to the rest of the app and to Python computations.

title: Streamlit Reference
text:
Layout and supporting evidence
with st.sidebar:
    year = st.selectbox("Year", [2020, 2023, 2025])

left, right = st.columns(2)
left.metric("Talks displayed", len(shown))
right.metric("Speakers represented", shown["speaker"].nunique())

with st.expander("Sources and interpretation"):
    st.write("Explain the sample, definitions, and limitations.")

st.link_button("Read the original talk", source_url)
An expander changes visibility. In the default behavior used here, putting code inside it does not make that computation wait until expansion.

title: Follow Along: Building the Explorer
text:
Day 1: a useful input
uv run streamlit run day1/01_basic.py
The file begins with familiar imports and a path relative to the script:
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
df = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/talks.csv")
__file__ is this script’s location. Its first parent is day1, and its second parent is the project root. This avoids a Windows-specific absolute path and does not depend on the browser’s filesystem.
Add the interface:
st.title("Explore conference messages")
year = st.select_slider(
    "Earliest conference year",
    options=[2020, 2023, 2025], value=2020,
)
shown = df.loc[df["year"] >= year]
st.metric("Talks displayed", f"{len(shown)} / {len(df)}")
st.bar_chart(shown.groupby("year").size().rename("Talks"))
st.dataframe(shown[["title", "speaker", "year", "kicker"]])

Day 1: observe execution
uv run streamlit run day1/02_execution.py
Predict before clicking. count = 0 runs again on every full script run. Each click on the first button displays 1. Changing and committing the name displays 0. print() appears in the terminal.

title: Follow Along: Building the Explorer
section: Day 2, step 1: display the existing analysis
text:
Day 2, step 1: display the existing analysis
Start with day2/app_live.py. It runs immediately as a small table app. Complete TODO 1 using day2/01_map.py as the checkpoint.
uv run streamlit run day2/app_live.py
After reading df, load the saved vectors and verify their alignment:
import numpy as np
import phate
import plotly.express as px

with np.load(ROOT / "data/talk_embeddings.npz", allow_pickle=False) as saved:
    assert np.array_equal(saved["talk_id"], df["talk_id"].to_numpy(dtype=str))
    assert np.array_equal(saved["kicker"], df["kicker"].to_numpy(dtype=str))
    X = saved["embeddings"]

coordinates = phate.PHATE(random_state=386).fit_transform(X)
df["PHATE1"] = coordinates[:, 0]
df["PHATE2"] = coordinates[:, 1]
This is the same analytical pattern as the previous lesson. No new embedding inference is needed when loading a saved array.
Display a first plot:
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="PHATE1", y="PHATE2", color="role_group",
    hover_name="title", hover_data=["speaker", "kicker"],
)
st.plotly_chart(fig, width="stretch")
One point is one short kicker. Use the plot to choose messages to read. The axes have no topic names.

text:
Step 2: a control changes the analysis view
The starter already contains a year multiselect and a filter. Move the plotting code below that filter and pass shown to px.scatter.
years = st.multiselect(
    "Conference years", [2020, 2023, 2025],
    default=[2020, 2023, 2025],
)
shown = df.loc[df["year"].isin(years)]

if shown.empty:
    st.info("Select a year to display messages.")
    st.stop()
Keep the full map’s frame:
fig.update_xaxes(range=[df["PHATE1"].min() - 0.1,
                        df["PHATE1"].max() + 0.1])
fig.update_yaxes(range=[df["PHATE2"].min() - 0.1,
                        df["PHATE2"].max() + 0.1])
The full app additionally assigns colors using the complete set of categories so a category keeps its color even when another disappears. Keeping coordinates fixed is separate from keeping automatic axis and color scales fixed.
Completed checkpoint:
uv run streamlit run day2/02_filters.py
Change a year and watch FITTING PHATE in the terminal. Explain why that repeated computation is unnecessary.

text:
Step 3: summaries explain the current view
a, b, c = st.columns(3)
a.metric("Talks displayed", f"{len(shown)} / {len(df)}")
b.metric("Speakers represented", shown["speaker"].nunique())
c.metric("Conferences represented",
         shown[["year", "month"]].drop_duplicates().shape[0])
Place summaries before the empty-result check if you want zeros to remain visible when the user selects nothing. The final app does this.
Choose another summary only if it supports the user’s question. Explain its denominator and which filters affect it.

title: Follow Along: Building the Explorer
text:
Step 4: cache a function result
Extract the PHATE computation into a function, above its first call:
@st.cache_data
def compute_map(X, random_state=386):
    print("CACHE MISS: fitting PHATE", flush=True)
    return phate.PHATE(random_state=random_state).fit_transform(X)

coordinates = compute_map(X)
Try a year filter again. The script still calls compute_map(X), but a matching cache entry supplies the coordinates without executing the body.
If PHATE runs quickly on your computer, use the isolated experiment:
uv run streamlit run day2/04_cache_lab.py
The delay is explicitly simulated and the returned value is a square. Try 2, 3, 2, then an unrelated display change.

title: Follow Along: Building the Explorer
text:
Step 5: cache input preparation
The finished loader accepts the small files’ contents:
from io import BytesIO

@st.cache_data
def load_inputs(csv_bytes, embedding_bytes):
    df = pd.read_csv(BytesIO(csv_bytes))
    with np.load(BytesIO(embedding_bytes), allow_pickle=False) as saved:
        assert np.array_equal(saved["talk_id"], df["talk_id"].to_numpy(dtype=str))
        assert np.array_equal(saved["kicker"], df["kicker"].to_numpy(dtype=str))
        X = saved["embeddings"].copy()
    return df, X

df, X = load_inputs(
    (ROOT / "data/talks.csv").read_bytes(),
    (ROOT / "data/talk_embeddings.npz").read_bytes(),
)
These files are small. Reading their bytes on a rerun makes freshness explicit. The cache reuses parsing and validation. Larger datasets call for a deliberate version or fingerprint strategy instead of reading everything on every interaction.
The reusable pipeline.py includes the same operations plus model, shape, and finite-value checks. The cached checkpoint imports it:
uv run streamlit run day2/03_cached.py

title: Follow Along: Building the Explorer
section: Step 6: connect the plot to evidence
text:
Step 6: connect the plot to evidence
For a short live version, add a displayed-talk selector and source link:
talk_id = st.selectbox("Choose a displayed talk", shown["talk_id"])
talk = shown.loc[shown["talk_id"].eq(talk_id)].iloc[0]
st.subheader(talk["title"])
st.write(talk["kicker"])
st.link_button("Read the original talk", talk["url"])
The final app formats selector labels as titles and speaker names, so readers do not need to recognize internal IDs.

title: Follow Along: Building the Explorer
text:
Completed app and optional extensions
uv run streamlit run app.py
The finished app includes speaker and role filters, literal text matching, stable categorical colors, source links, downloads, and a similarity-ranking expander. Similarity uses the original 768-dimensional vectors, excludes the chosen talk, and ranks only the other currently displayed records.
The keyword input performs a literal text match. It does not embed the query or claim to perform semantic search.
For the optional local embedding cache, start Ollama and pull Nomic first:
ollama pull nomic-embed-text:v1.5
uv run streamlit run day2/05_local_embedding.py
Submit the same message twice, then a changed message. A form batches the inputs until Submit. The function’s arguments are text, model, and prefix. The decorator caches returned vectors, while Ollama manages its own model process.

Warm-up: our existing Plotly figure
Our published conference map already supports hover, zoom, and legend interaction.
With a partner:

What can a reader investigate without running Python?
What would still require changing our notebook?

section: Think, pair, share: does this need an app?
text:
Think, pair, share: does this need an app?

A classmate needs one figure for tomorrow’s presentation.
A librarian repeatedly compares use across branches and dates.
A researcher wants to inspect model outputs and their source records.

Choose one. What would an app make easier? What would you ask the user first?

Allow two minutes. A dashboard has development and maintenance costs. Cases 2 and 3 have plausible recurring interaction. In case 1, a clear figure is likely sufficient. Accept alternatives supported by a specific user task.

title: Useful Dashboards

Why Streamlit fits this course
We can reuse pandas transformations and existing Plotly figures.
A widget returns a Python value. We use that value in our analysis, then display the result.
The application supplies the browser interface without requiring us to write its HTML or JavaScript.

Streamlit documentation: https://docs.streamlit.io/get-started/fundamentals/main-concepts . Frame this as a good match for Python data apps. More customized web workflows may justify other frameworks.

The default execution model

Run the script from top to bottom.
Display the Streamlit elements in the browser.

title: Useful Dashboards
text:
Predict the next run
print("START")
count = 0
name = st.text_input("Your name", "Ada")
if st.button("Add one"):
    count += 1
st.write(count)
What appears after clicking Add one twice? What happens after changing the name?

Run day1/02_execution.py. On initial run count is 0. Each button click starts a fresh run and displays 1, not an accumulated total. Editing the name and committing it displays 0. text:
Prepared outputs and a reproducible workflow
The project includes genuine saved Nomic embeddings.
Their artifact records the text, ordered talk IDs, model, and prefix.
Preparation code and provenance explain how to regenerate them. The hosted app can use them without running Ollama.

The supplied vectors use the official Nomic quantized ONNX export. data/embedding_provenance.json records the exact revision, hashes, backend, and pooling. The previous lesson used Ollama. These are genuine outputs of the same named model with a different inference backend, so exact vectors and PHATE layouts can differ. Import previous vectors using scripts/prepare_data.py if matching the previous map is important. Students do not need ONNX dependencies for the app.

)
assert np.array_equal(
    saved["kicker"], df["kicker"].to_numpy(dtype=str)
)
A vector must remain attached to the text that produced it.
Sorting only one file can create a plausible picture with incorrect labels.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Meaningful filters
years = st.multiselect(
    "Conference years", [2020, 2023, 2025],
    default=[2020, 2023, 2025],
)
shown = df.loc[df["year"].isin(years)]
Use shown for the map and its supporting records.
An empty selection means no years. Tell the reader how to recover.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Metrics for the current view
With a partner, propose a useful summary.
What question does it answer? Does it describe the full sample or the filtered records?
Our starting choices:

Talks displayed out of the full sample
Unique speakers represented
Distinct conferences represented


Two minutes. A conference is a year-month combination, not just a year. The full sample has 52 talks, 35 speakers, and 6 conferences. All numbers should update together. An average kicker length is defensible only when connected to a question about the represented text.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
A summary row
a, b, c = st.columns(3)
a.metric("Talks displayed", f"{len(shown)} / {len(df)}")
b.metric("Speakers represented", shown["speaker"].nunique())
c.metric("Conferences represented",
         shown[["year", "month"]].drop_duplicates().shape[0])
For 2025: 16 / 52 talks, 16 speakers, 2 conferences.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Filtering and refitting
Our app fits the full sample once, then filters the displayed rows.
The original coordinates, axis ranges, and color assignments remain stable.
Refitting PHATE on a subset would ask a different question and create a different map. Keep that as a separate analysis choice.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
section: Observation: an unrelated input feels slow
text:
Observation: an unrelated input feels slow
uv run streamlit run day2/02_filters.py
Watch the terminal while changing the year selection.
Why does FITTING PHATE appear again?
Which result could we reuse?

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
section: A function call can reuse its result

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Cache hit or cache miss?



Change
Cached PHATE result?




Color points by another metadata field
Reuse


Filter which full-map points appear
Reuse


Supply different embedding vectors
Recompute


Change the random-state argument
Recompute


Clear this function’s cache
Recompute on the next call



Explain each answer using the function’s inputs.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
A short cache experiment
uv run streamlit run day2/04_cache_lab.py
Predict, then try:

Select 2, then 3, then 2 again.
Change only the display preference.
Clear the cache and repeat.

The one-second delay is deliberately simulated. The result is ordinary arithmetic.

Use this for three minutes if PHATE is too fast to demonstrate timing clearly. It isolates caching from the statistical method. Do not imply the delay simulates actual measured inference time.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Caching the actual pipeline



Work
Treatment




Load and validate saved data
st.cache_data


Compute the full PHATE map
st.cache_data


Apply cheap filters and summaries
Recalculate


Load a Python model or connection object
Often st.cache_resource



Our deployed app loads embedding arrays. It does not load an embedding model.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Cache, session, or saved artifact?



Need
Mechanism




Reuse an expensive function result
Data cache


Reuse a model or connection object
Resource cache


Remember this user’s additional choices
Session State


Keep model outputs across app restarts
Saved artifact



By default, caches can serve multiple users. User-specific memory belongs in the appropriate session mechanism.

Source: https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/caching . Cached data returns copies. Cached resources normally share the same object and require care with mutation and concurrency. Scope configuration exists, but is outside this introduction. A cache is not a durable project data store.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Freshness is an input-design problem
Our finished loader receives the actual file contents:
df, X = load_inputs(
    csv_path.read_bytes(),
    embedding_path.read_bytes(),
)
Changed contents produce a different cache key.
A cached function given only a filename will not automatically notice every change to that file.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Live sources and local embeddings
For a changing external source, a lifetime can limit stale results:
@st.cache_data(ttl=600)
def fetch_data(url):
    ...
After expiration, a subsequent call refreshes the result. This is not a scheduled data pipeline.
An optional local app caches a real embedding call by text, model, and prefix.

Only show day2/05_local_embedding.py if Ollama is prepared. The core hosted app never requires it. A Streamlit cache of returned vectors does not manage the Ollama server’s loaded-model memory. Source: https://docs.ollama.com/api/embed .

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Evidence behind the map
The completed app connects the visual view to:

A selected kicker and its author
An original source link
Supporting records for the current filters
An optional ranking using original-vector cosine similarity

Read messages before naming a theme. The 2D map can distort relationships.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Deployment changes where Python runs







Location
Role




GitHub repository
Stores code, data artifacts, and dependency definitions


Streamlit Community Cloud
Installs dependencies and runs Python


Reader’s browser
Displays and interacts with the app


GitHub Pages
Hosts our static project website, which can link to the app




Sources: https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/architecture and https://docs.streamlit.io/deploy/streamlit-community-cloud/deploy-your-app/deploy . Push the supplied small embedding artifact. Never push the local .venv directory or model weights.

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
The deployment workflow

Run app.py locally and check its filters.
Commit and push code, data, pyproject.toml, and uv.lock.
Open share.streamlit.io and create an app.
Select the repository, branch, and app.py.
Choose Python 3.12, deploy, and inspect the logs.

Community Cloud recognizes uv.lock. Use the same environment definition locally and on the host.

Reserve 10-12 minutes. Sources: https://docs.streamlit.io/deploy/streamlit-community-cloud/deploy-your-app/app-dependencies and https://docs.streamlit.io/deploy/streamlit-community-cloud/deploy-your-app/deploy . The exact UI wording may change. Follow deployment.qmd. If accounts block a student, pair them with a deployed app and complete the task-based check.

section: A small update completes the loop
text:
A small update completes the loop
Change a useful label, commit, and push to the app’s selected branch.
Check the deployed result and logs.
Ask a partner to answer the original question using only the interface.
Could they identify relevant messages and verify the source?

title: A Shareable Text Explorer
text:
Exit check

Why can changing a color reuse the PHATE result?
What distinguishes saved embeddings from a runtime cache?
Where does Python run after deployment?
Which interface choice made the analysis easier to use?

Keep the reproducible workflow visible in the repository and the reader’s task clear in the app.

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
1. Run the completed app locally
From the project root:
uv sync --locked
uv run streamlit run app.py
Check all years, only 2025, and no years. Expected talk counts are 52, 16, and 0. Open a source link and check that the supporting table agrees with the plot.

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
2. Commit and push the project
If using an existing repository, copy the contents of the extracted project into that repository’s root. Keep its existing Git history. Use git status to inspect changes before committing.
If creating a new repository, create an empty GitHub repository, clone it with its actual URL, copy these project contents into the clone, and run these commands from the clone:
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add conference message explorer"
git push
The supplied .gitignore excludes .venv, Python caches, and .streamlit/secrets.toml. Keep it when copying the project. Include:

app.py and pipeline.py
data/talks.csv, data/talk_embeddings.npz, and provenance/source notes
pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version

The rest of the teaching website can remain in the same repository. Do not upload downloaded model weights or the .venv directory.
Community Cloud recognizes uv.lock. Keep the matching pyproject.toml alongside it. You do not need an additional requirements.txt. The optional preparation dependency group is for rebuilding model outputs, not for normal app startup.

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
3. Create the app
At share.streamlit.io, create a new app from an existing GitHub repository. Select:



Setting
Value




Repository
Your repository containing this project


Branch
The branch you pushed, commonly main


Main file path
app.py when the project is at the repository root


Python version
3.12, matching the project


Secrets
Leave empty for this demo



If the project lives in a subfolder, use its actual entrypoint path and keep its uv.lock and pyproject.toml together next to that entrypoint. The root layout is simplest for this lesson.
Deploy and read the logs. The host installs the project dependencies, then runs your app. The local uv run streamlit run app.py command is for your terminal. Community Cloud supplies the server launch.
See the official deployment walkthrough if button labels change.

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
4. Check it as a reader
Open the app’s streamlit.app URL in another browser session. Confirm that the intended audience can access it. Have someone else use the interface to answer the original question.
GitHub stores the repository. Community Cloud runs Python. Readers need a browser. Their laptop does not need your uv environment or Ollama.

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
5. Update it
Change a meaningful label, commit, and push to the app’s selected branch. Community Cloud updates the app from that repository. Watch the logs and verify the change at the hosted URL. A dependency change can require rebuilding the environment.
Link this app from the project’s GitHub Pages website. GitHub Pages hosts static HTML and cannot run this Python server.

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
Common failures







Symptom
What to check




Cannot find the repository
GitHub account, repository permissions, and organization authorization


Missing Python package
Correct lockfile and pyproject committed next to the entrypoint


Python version conflict
Select Python 3.12 on Community Cloud


Missing CSV or NPZ
Data files committed, exact filename case, and repository location


Vector alignment error
Matching talk IDs, row order, text, model, and prefix


Works locally with Ollama, fails remotely
Deploy app.py, which loads saved vectors, rather than the optional local embedding app


Slow first visit
Cold start and initial PHATE computation. Subsequent compatible calls can reuse cached results


New external data does not appear
Cache input/version design or expiration policy

title: Deployment with uv, GitHub, and Community Cloud
text:
Secrets in other projects
This demo needs none. For a project that needs credentials, keep the local .streamlit/secrets.toml out of Git and enter secrets through the host’s settings. A password or token in a public repository becomes public. Do not add an authentication system to this lesson’s demo merely to practice deployment.

title: Instructor Guide
text:
Students should be able to justify an interface choice using a reader’s task, trace a basic Streamlit rerun, identify reusable computation, and deploy a small app from a reproducible repository.

title: Instructor Guide
text:
Suggested answers

Format choice
A single presentation figure usually needs a clear label and explanation. Repeated comparisons across branches and dates benefit from controls. Inspecting model outputs benefits from a summary connected to source records. Accept alternatives when students specify a concrete need.


Rerun prediction
In day1/02_execution.py, the first counter starts at 0 on every run. Its button click makes it 1 for that run. Two clicks still display 1. Editing and committing the name displays 0. The Session State counter persists across this session’s reruns. A new tab has a separate session.
print() writes to the Python server’s terminal or hosted logs. st.write() displays in the app.


Cache dependencies







Change
What needs new analytical results?




Color field
Figure styling changes. Data and full-sample coordinates can be reused


Displayed year subset
Filter and summaries change. Full-sample vectors and map can be reused


One kicker changes
That embedding needs regeneration and the full-data PHATE fit needs recomputation. The alignment check should reject a mismatched old artifact


PHATE random-state argument
The map needs a new fit, while loading and embeddings can be reused



The supplied regeneration script deliberately rebuilds all 52 embeddings for a simple visible workflow. A larger production pipeline could persist outputs per text/model/prefix and update only changed records. Adding @st.cache_data to a per-text embedding call demonstrates that idea within a running app.


Cache experiment
With caching enabled, the first call for 2 is a miss, then 3 is a miss, then 2 is a hit. An unrelated preference change calls the function with the same input and should hit. Clearing the cache makes the next call a miss. Previously cached entries may exist from earlier demonstrations. Clear the function’s cache before the exercise.


Metrics and interpretation
Full sample: 52 talks, 35 speakers, 6 conferences. Years 2023 and 2025: 36, 28, 4. Only 2025: 16, 16, 2. Count conferences as year-month pairs.
The sample is purposive, with short kickers rather than full talk bodies. A count change across years does not establish archive trends. A PHATE cluster-looking region is a reason to read the texts, not proof of a topic or natural group. Similarity rankings use original-vector cosine similarity and exclude the selected talk.


Cache, state, and artifact
The data cache reuses function results. A resource cache normally reuses an object such as an in-process Python model. Session State holds additional per-session values. The saved NPZ artifact keeps model outputs across restarts and carries identifiers/provenance. Ollama’s server process is outside Python’s resource cache.

title: Instructor Guide
text:
Reusing the earlier embeddings
The original EDA archive provided saving code rather than a saved embedding file. This package therefore includes genuine Nomic inference produced using the model owner’s quantized ONNX export. It records the exact revision, hashes, prefix, and postprocessing in data/embedding_provenance.json. These outputs can differ numerically from Ollama and change a nonlinear layout. No need to teach ONNX in class.
To preserve the exact earlier output, import your saved talk_embeddings.npz using the command in the README. The script checks text and ID alignment. Rerender app screenshots if you need them to match that earlier map exactly.

title: Instructor Guide
section: Teaching choices carried over from the original resources
text:
Teaching choices carried over from the original resources
The updated lessons retain the focus on questions, sensible defaults, context, sources, reproducibility, and Python-first development. They add a visible execution trace and a task-based evaluation. Reverse proxies, load balancing, authentication systems, multipage navigation, and background workers remain outside the main two-day route.
Use the cheatsheet as a reference. Introduce only the commands needed for the next useful change.
